query: My doctor found a kidney stone. How do they get rid of it?
final_answer: If a stone will not pass on its own, doctors can use shock waves to break it into smaller pieces [1]. They may also insert a scope through the urethra to reach the stone [1]. In some situations, surgery is performed to take the stone out [1]. Hospital treatments may include shock wave lithotripsy (SWL) [3]. Larger or obstructing stones can be removed with a ureteroscope or by percutaneous nephrolithotomy [3].

query: Why would someone keep wheezing, coughing, and feel tightness in their chest?
final_answer: Persistent wheezing, coughing, and chest tightness can be symptoms of acute bronchitis, which often follows a cold or flu and may last for weeks [1]. Chronic bronchitis also includes coughing, wheezing, and chest discomfort as common signs [1]. Asthma commonly causes coughing, wheezing, and a feeling of chest tightness [3].

query: What tests do doctors use to check for Alzheimer's?
final_answer: Doctors may ask about overall health, past medical problems, ability to carry out daily activities, and changes in behavior and personality [1]. They conduct tests to measure memory, problem solving, attention, counting, and language skills [1]. They carry out standard medical tests, such as blood and urine tests [1]. They perform brain scans to look for anything in the brain that does not look normal [1]. The only definitive way to diagnose Alzheimer’s disease is to find plaques and tangles in brain tissue, which is done by brain autopsy after death [1].

final_answer: Most cases of Prader‑Willi syndrome are not inherited, especially when caused by a deletion in the paternal chromosome 15 or by maternal uniparental disomy[1]. These genetic changes occur as random events during the formation of reproductive cells or early embryonic development, so affected people usually have no family history of the disorder[1]. Rarely, a genetic change that inactivates genes on the paternal chromosome 15 can be passed from one generation to the next[1]. The risk to family members depends on the specific genetic cause of the condition[2].

final_answer: Huntington disease is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, meaning one altered copy of the HTT gene is enough to cause the disorder [1]. An affected person usually inherits the altered gene from an affected parent, and each child of a person with Huntington disease has a 50% chance of inheriting the mutated gene [2]. In rare cases the disease can arise from a new (de novo) mutation, so a person may have no affected parent [2]. As the gene is passed down, the CAG repeat often expands, leading to earlier onset in later generations, a phenomenon called anticipation [1].

Crohn disease is linked to genetic variations on chromosomes 5 and 10, including the IBD5 locus on chromosome 5 and other regions called “gene deserts” that may regulate nearby genes[1]. Specific gene variants that increase risk include ATG16L1, IRGM, NOD2, and IL23R, which provide instructions for proteins involved in immune system function[1]. These genetic changes may affect how intestinal cells respond to bacteria, potentially leading to chronic inflammation[1]. The inheritance pattern of Crohn disease is unclear because many genetic and environmental factors are likely involved, but the disease tends to cluster in families[2].

MELAS is caused by mutations in mitochondrial DNA and is therefore transmitted by maternal (mitochondrial) inheritance. [1] Only egg cells, not sperm cells, provide mitochondria to the developing embryo, so only females can pass the mutation to their children. [1] Because of this pattern, MELAS can appear in every generation of a family and affect both males and females. [1] In most cases the altered mitochondrial gene is inherited from the mother, but less commonly the condition results from a new mutation with no family history. [1]

query: What condition is linked to mutations in the DMD gene?
final_answer: Mutations in the DMD gene cause Duchenne muscular dystrophy, a rapidly progressive form of muscular dystrophy that mainly affects boys [1]. Duchenne muscular dystrophy leads to progressive loss of muscle function and weakness, beginning in the lower limbs and can also affect the heart [1]. The same DMD gene mutations also cause Becker muscular dystrophy, a milder form where some functional dystrophin is produced [4]. Both conditions are classified as dystrophinopathies because they result from faulty or missing dystrophin [4].

query: What condition is linked to mutations in the PAH gene?
final_answer: Mutations in the PAH gene cause phenylketonuria. [2] The PAH gene provides instructions for making the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase. [2] When these gene mutations reduce the activity of phenylalanine hydroxylase, phenylalanine can build up to toxic levels and may damage the brain. [2]

query: What condition is linked to mutations in the TSC1 gene?
final_answer: Mutations in the TSC1 gene can cause tuberous sclerosis complex. [1] Tuberous sclerosis complex has an autosomal dominant pattern, and one altered copy of the TSC1 gene increases the risk of tumors and other developmental problems. [2] Mutations in the TSC1 gene also cause lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM). [3] LAM involves tumors and cysts in the lungs that result from loss of functional hamartin. [3]

query: What condition is linked to mutations in the ABCD1 gene?
final_answer: Mutations in the ABCD1 gene cause X‑linked adrenoleukodystrophy. [1] The disorder is inherited in an X‑linked pattern, meaning the mutated gene is located on the X chromosome. [3] Males with one altered copy of the ABCD1 gene develop the disease, while females usually have milder or later‑onset features. [3] The disease involves accumulation of very long‑chain fatty acids that can damage the adrenal cortex and myelin. [1]
